items.title: Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
items.publisher: European Commission (AI Office); drafted by independent chairs
items.why: Source of the quotation. Voluntary. Two layers (digitally signed metadata plus imperceptible watermark) for audio, image, video and containerised text; watermark alone for free-form text; fingerprinting or logging optional and not sufficient alone. Published 10 June 2026; found adequate by the Commission on 8 July 2026. Linked from digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/code-practice-ai-generated-content.
items.quote: relying on fingerprinting or logging alone is not considered sufficient

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 50: Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Article 50(2) and 50(4); see also Article 2(1)(a) and (c) on the same site
items.why: The marking duty on providers and the disclosure duty on deployers. This is the Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned empty pages). The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the displayed text is not yet updated; paragraphs 2 and 4 are not flagged as amended.
items.quote: shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 111: AI systems already placed on the market
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Article 111(4), marked NEW; with Article 113 (general application from 2 August 2026)
items.why: Source of the dates. Systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with the marking duty by 2 December 2026. Commission's copy; carries the same 'not yet updated' notice although the new paragraph is displayed.
items.quote: shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026

items.title: Deepfake Defences 2: The Attribution Toolkit
items.locator: Key takeaways 5 and 8 (pp. 6-7); Box 2 (p. 14); survey findings (pp. 25-26)
items.why: Source of the figure. A discussion paper, not guidance: Ofcom says regulated services are not required to adopt the measures. Says watermarks, metadata and labels should be used in combination.
items.quote: Attribution measures should be used in combination to tackle the greatest range of deepfakes.

items.title: Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Intellectual Property Office
items.locator: Section E: Output transparency (Overview; Conclusions and proposals); summary under 'Labelling of AI and human-created content'
items.why: The UK position in the government's own words: no obligation to label AI-generated content; proposal to work with industry on good practice. Published 18 March 2026.
items.quote: some developers and service providers provide labelling services and tools in the UK

items.title: Disclosure of AI in Advertising: Striking the Balance Between Creativity and Responsibility
items.publisher: Advertising Standards Authority and Committee of Advertising Practice
items.why: No blanket UK requirement to disclose AI in adverts; existing rules apply however content is made; a disclosure does not cure a misleading claim. An advice article, not a Code rule.
items.quote: There is no blanket legal requirement in the UK to disclose the use of AI in ads

items.title: Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of the AI Act, C(2026) 5054 final, Annex
items.locator: Section 4.2, paragraph 70; marking obligation defined at 4.2.1, paragraph 71
items.quote: For every marking solution deployed, providers should ensure that corresponding means for detection are available
items.why: The Commission's reading of the marking duty: two linked elements, marking and detectability, and marking without a way to detect it 'will not suffice'. Supports 'detection capability maintained' in the top level. Non-binding; content approved 20 July 2026 with formal adoption to follow once all language versions exist. The PDF itself, linked from the Commission's library page.

items.title: California Senate Bill No. 942 (California AI Transparency Act), Chapter 291, Statutes of 2024
items.locator: Section 1, adding Business and Professions Code s.22757.3(b)
items.quote: A covered provider shall include a latent disclosure in AI-generated image, video, or audio content
items.why: Comparator: a US state statute that requires a machine-readable ('latent') mark, an optional visible one (s.22757.3(a)) and a free public detection tool (s.22757.2). Text is not among the content types listed. Applies only to generative systems with over 1,000,000 monthly users. Chaptered text as enacted in 2024; later amendments and the operative date were not checked. US state law.

items.title: Reducing Risks Posed by Synthetic Content: An Overview of Technical Approaches to Digital Content Transparency (NIST AI 100-4)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: none of these techniques can be considered as a comprehensive solution; the value of any given technique is use-case and context specific
items.why: The fullest public technical survey of watermarking, metadata and detection, with the known ways each fails (compression, cropping, paraphrase). Evidence for layered marking and for testing robustness instead of trusting a supplier. A technical overview, not a standard or a rule; US federal agency.

items.title: Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification, version 2.4
items.publisher: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
items.quote: A digitally signed and tamper-evident data structure that references a set of assertions
items.why: The open industry specification for signed provenance metadata, the kind of 'digitally signed metadata' the EU code asks for as one layer. Free to read. An industry consortium specification, not a formal national or international standard on the page read; the research log records that the EU code does not name it. Version 2.4 (April 2026) was the latest found; check for a newer one.

items.title: Public content provenance for organisations
items.publisher: National Cyber Security Centre and Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
items.quote: Digital watermarking is not a provenance mechanism but is included here because it is often considered for addressing digital trust challenges.
items.why: The UK's technical authority on what provenance tools can and cannot prove. Useful corrective: a watermark shows a signal is present, not where content came from, so it complements signed metadata and does not replace it. A primer for security and communications teams, written for organisations proving their own content is genuine, not for marking AI output; no duty attached. Date taken from the NCSC collection page.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 7 (You are open and collaborative), practical recommendations
items.quote: Clearly signpost when AI has been used to create content, is interacting with members of the public, or is used in decision-making processes
items.why: The nearest thing to a UK labelling expectation: government tells its own departments to signpost AI-made content. Visible signposting only; says nothing about machine-readable marks. Public-sector guidance, not a duty on companies.

items.title: A Watermark for Large Language Models
items.publisher: Kirchenbauer, Geiping, Wen, Katz, Miers and Goldstein, arXiv:2301.10226 (ICML 2023)
items.quote: embedding signals into generated text that are invisible to humans but algorithmically detectable from a short span of tokens
items.why: The paper that set out how text watermarking works in practice, and the basis for much of what the EU code calls an imperceptible watermark for text. Peer reviewed at a conference (ICML 2023); the arXiv copy is the authors' own. Tests on one model family; robustness is discussed, not guaranteed.

items.title: Scalable watermarking for identifying large language model outputs
items.quote: Watermarking can help identify synthetic text and limit accidental or deliberate misuse
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Reports a production-ready text watermark that, on the authors' evaluation, preserves text quality, so 'technically feasible' is no longer hypothetical for text. The paper describes its authors' own system; the abstract itself notes watermarking had not been adopted in production before.

items.title: Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?
items.publisher: Sadasivan, Kumar, Balasubramanian, Wang and Feizi, arXiv:2303.11156
items.quote: while our recursive paraphrasing method can significantly reduce detection rates, it only slightly degrades text quality in many cases
items.why: The counter-evidence a board should hear: paraphrasing defeats several text detectors, watermark-based ones included, and human-written text can be made to look machine-made. Supports testing robustness and not treating detection as proof. Preprint (version 4, January 2025); attack results on passages of about 300 tokens.

items.title: Invisible Image Watermarks Are Provably Removable Using Generative AI
items.quote: we demonstrate that pixel-level invisible watermarks are vulnerable to this regeneration attack
items.why: Peer reviewed at a conference (NeurIPS 2024). Shows with proofs and tests on four schemes that pixel-level image watermarks can be removed by adding noise and regenerating the image; consistent with Ofcom's cropping finding. Says watermarks that keep the image semantically similar may resist. Laboratory attacks, not measured misuse.
